documents.abstract: Neoliberalism has re-engineered education into a market-driven, performance-oriented system that prioritizes standardised metrics over a spirit of inquiry. This article explores how this shift undermines teachers’ teaching abilities, highly impacts their self-efficacy and compromises students' achievement motivation. To counteract this rigid framework, the following article argues that educators must cultivate symbiotic classroom relationships and prioritize social-emotional learning. Doing so, it is essential to liberate cognitive engagement and rescue holistic academic outcomes from corporate constraints. While it is necessary to prepare individuals for jobs and realistic challenges, it is also crucial to focus on the achievement motivation of the students keeping in mind the individual differences and tempering their responsiveness to demanding situations. It also highlights the need to take a critical approach towards the academic performance of the students in the academic settings by looking at it from the psychological lens.

Many studies in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) have explored the tactile experience of material textures for its potential in virtual reality and tangible interaction. We introduce TesselTex, an inflatable silicone-based structure, consisting of a tessellated matrix of textured “pixel”s made from two materials with differing roughness. By inflating embedded air chambers, skin contact between different materials on the tessellated surface can be adjusted, thereby modulating users’ tactile perception of textures. We investigated how users perceived fine roughness and surface bumpiness under different pneumatically-controlled “pixel” heights, with TesselTex samples of different “pixel” densities and material compositions, in active (finger) and passive (forearm) stroking interactions. Results showed that pneumatic lifting of the material “pixels” significantly decreased user-perceived roughness in composite samples, an effect not observed in conventional single-material bump arrays. Meanwhile, “pixel” lifting significantly increased perceived surface bumpiness during active finger exploration, but had slight opposite effect under passive forearm stroking. In addition, higher “pixel” density slightly increased the perceived roughness of the surface and modulated bumpiness perception, depending on the interaction mode.

documents.abstract: The Artist of Tomorrow: Conductor or Mere Performer? An Interdisciplinary Exploratory Review of Human Creativity, Artificial Intelligence, and Copyright Law This interdisciplinary exploratory review examines the evolving role of human creativity in an era of artificial intelligence, automation, and digital artistic production. Through a historical perspective spanning several centuries, the study explores major technological and artistic transitions, including photography, cinema, sound recording, conceptual art, digital editing, and generative artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to the distinction between technical execution and human creative intention, examining how artistic originality may emerge through selection, composition, interpretation, and creative direction rather than manual production alone. The review also addresses legal questions surrounding copyright protection, public-domain works, AI-assisted restoration, and human authorship, drawing on French, European, and American legal frameworks. A case study involving the 1925 film The Phantom of the Opera illustrates the complexities of audiovisual restoration, original musical contributions, and derivative creative elements. The HUMAN.zip exploratory framework further examines human–AI collaboration, highlighting methodological limitations, interpretative biases, and opportunities for future comparative research. Central hypothesis: "Automating execution does not necessarily mean automating creation." This publication aims to contribute to interdisciplinary discussions on artistic authorship, technological transformation, intellectual property, and the future relationship between human creativity and artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human Creativity, Copyright Law, Artistic Originality, Human–AI Collaboration, Digital Art, Cinema History, Public Domain, Generative AI, HUMAN.zip. Publication type: Exploratory interdisciplinary review. Date: November 20, 2026.

documents.abstract: Contemporary theorising about the ethical dimensions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicates at least two problematic tendencies. The first is a default focus on a narrow range of moral concepts, such as autonomy, justice, and fairness, to the occlusion of a wider range of concepts. The second is a 'bright siding' focus on concepts that track the positive dimensions of moral practice and experience, such as virtue, flourishing, solutionism, moral progress and the good life. Taken together, the consequence is the production of large-scale moral frameworks which systematically fail to accommodate negative dimensions of moral life (Jobin et al, 2019). Two main symptoms are a one-sided focus on virtues and excellences at the expense of vices and failings and the other is an affirmation of the edifying potential of new technologies without due appreciation of their corruptive potential (Coeckelberg, 2020. p.59). Drawing on the example of Higher Education research and knowledge production, we suggest that a more comprehensive assessment of the moral possibilities of new technologies requires greater inclusion of a negatively toned, vice-informed range of moral concepts, narratives and sensibilities. We elucidate these points by providing examples of techno-vice in everyday life. This helps to elucidate the concept of epistemic vices and the phenomenon of corruption which, we argue, inform the concept of technomoral-vices.

documents.abstract: Generative AI redistributes the work of producing and evaluating knowledge in teacher-designed learning tasks, but how students retain direction while judging its outputs remains unclear. We examined how teacher instructions and materials enter student–GenAI dialogue, how reasoning display and web search relate to interaction time, what students evaluate and verify, and how groups coordinate systems. We analysed 81 screen recordings from 29 graduate student groups completing educational design tasks, coding 1,149 events and 275 prompts. Students relayed task requirements, steered successive requests and transferred outputs across platforms. Task directives persisted across turns, whereas references to course materials declined and elaboration requests increased. Reasoning display and web search were each associated with approximately 65% longer machine turns and a 19-percentage-point larger machine share of coded interaction time. Across 150 turns displaying reasoning and 86 with web retrieval, the recordings showed no reopening of a reasoning trace or inspection of a cited source. Students corrected pedagogical fit while asking the machine to assure factual accuracy. These findings distinguish control over the dialogue from responsibility for establishing credibility. Learning tasks can make that responsibility visible by requiring students to justify a consequential claim against its source or course material before using it.

documents.abstract: Visualization backgrounds in optical-see-through augmented-reality (OST-AR) consist of the user’s immediate environment, which introduces unique design challenges for colour-coded visualizations. Yet, there exist limited guidelines on how to design interpretable colour encodings in OST-AR based on the user’s viewing conditions (e.g., minimum contrast between the OST-AR marks and the background). We present the results of two controlled lab experiments (N = 18 each) – one with physical surfaces as background, one with an opaque display simulating the same surfaces – quantifying how viewing conditions affect the interpretability of colour-coded scatterplots in OST-AR. Our study results show that luminance contrast can degrade interpretation performance when Michelson contrast drops below \(34\%\). We also observe colour-encoding interpretability and user experience significantly worsen when backgrounds include two main colours (up to \(49\%\) longer interpretations, and \(20\%\) lower accuracy). However, we do not find any evidence that poor chromatic contrast degrades interpretability, contrasting with common opaque-display visualization practices. Taken together, our findings provide insights on key factors of viewing conditions that limit the interpretability of colour encodings – which we consolidate into three design guidelines – and offer preliminary support for the simulation of viewing conditions through opaque displays to study colour-encoding interpretability in OST-AR.

Enterprise security programs are built on the assumption that defended systems stay fixed between periodic reviews. Autonomous AI agents break that assumption because they decide at runtime which tools, peers, and data to access, and so redraw their own attack surface. Existing maturity instruments, including the Capability Maturity Model, COBIT-based assessment, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, were built to grade human-run practices that change slowly. Newer agent-specific governance models treat adaptive control as the top of a single scale rather than as an independently scored dimension. Two documented incidents, an external agent that reportedly reached McKinsey’s production database within about two hours, and a zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that enabled data exfiltration through a single email, show that periodic assessment cannot keep pace with a system that redraws its own scope in the moment. This paper proposes a four-dimension, five-level maturity model comprising Visibility, Containment, Accountability, and Adaptability, each anchored to an observable test rather than a self-reported survey response. Applied to a composite financial advisory firm, the model scores each dimension independently rather than averaging them, surfacing an imbalance (strong detection, weak prevention) that a composite score would conceal, and yielding a prioritized remediation order that supports business sustainability. The framework is presented as a structured self-assessment instrument, with a defined pathway for expert review, inter-rater testing, and pilot evaluation. The model has not yet been validated against real organizations, and its Adaptability dimension remains constrained by the current state of governance tooling.

This article examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in shaping students' academic development within contemporary educational systems. It analyzes how intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, and large language models foster personalized learning, accelerate academic research, enhance writing proficiency, and bridge educational equity gaps. Simultaneously, the paper evaluates the pedagogical challenges associated with AI integration, including cognitive over-reliance, algorithmic bias, and academic integrity concerns, demonstrating that human-centered mentorship and AI literacy are vital for sustainable intellectual growth.

documents.abstract: The role of digital innovation and artificial intelligence in contemporary schooling is examined in this research paper. It emphasizes how cutting-edge teaching techniques, digital platforms, and AI-powered technology enhance learning quality, boost student engagement, and facilitate individualized instruction. The benefits, difficulties, and prospects for incorporating AI into educational systems are also covered in the paper.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced so quickly that it has drastically changed the educational landscape by changing the roles of both educators and learners and providing novel techniques to language learning. Personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated assessment, and the improvement of learners' communicative ability are all made possible by the integration of AI into English Language Teaching (ELT), which has emerged as a potential pedagogical advancement. Intelligent tutoring systems, conversational chatbots, automated writing assessment tools, and speech recognition technologies are just a few examples of AI-powered applications that give students instant feedback, allow them to practice language interactively, and better meet their unique language needs. These technologies also have the ability to support learner autonomy, enable individualized instruction, and make English language training more accessible in a variety of educational settings.Despite these benefits, integrating AI into ELT poses a number of technological, ethical, and pedagogical difficulties. The efficacy and sustainability of AI-mediated language learning are called into doubt by issues with data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, the correctness and dependability of AI-generated information, and an over-reliance on automated systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is not new to knowledge management (KM) research, but generative AI (GenAI) shifts AI’s role from supporting knowledge work to producing knowledge artifacts. We examine how research in one established KM community, the Knowledge, Innovation, and Entrepreneurial Systems (KIES) track of the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS), has changed alongside this shift. In a systematic mapping study, we analyze all 319 papers published in the track between 2020 and 2026, classified with an AI-supported, source-grounded pipeline into three AI-relevance tiers (CORE, PARTIAL, NONE). The CORE share rises from 16.2% in 2020 to 29.8% in 2024 and jumps to 58.5% in 2025 and 66.7% in 2026; since the number of papers per year remains roughly constant, AI research takes the place of other topics and spreads across nearly all mini-tracks. We interpret this shift through three emerging stories (AI moving from tool to collaborator, trust from user perception to system design, and knowledge from human to hybrid artifacts) and suggest that KM research in this track is changing with GenAI but was, in part, prepared for it by its history. For research, the findings call for empirical studies of hybrid human–AI knowledge work, design research on validation and epistemic friction, system-level measures of trustworthiness, and extensions of theories such as Nonaka’s SECI model and the knowledge-based view with constructs such as provenance and validation chains. For practice, they suggest building deliberate friction, such as review and source-checking steps, into AI-supported knowledge work and tracking which knowledge artifacts are AI-generated and who validated them.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing higher education by changing the ways universities teach, assess students, provide academic support, and conduct research. AI-based tools can personalise learning, offer immediate formative feedback, improve accessibility, support language learning, and reduce repetitive administrative tasks. However, these opportunities are accompanied by important risks, including inaccurate or fabricated information, algorithmic bias, privacy and security concerns, unequal access to technology, academic misconduct, and excessive dependence on automated assistance. This article examines major applications of AI in higher education, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and outlines principles for responsible implementation, particularly for universities in Uzbekistan.

documents.abstract: This study examines the role of the technologies under investigation expert systems, machine learning, and blockchain in enhancing accountants’ professional competence in light of International Education Standard 6 (IES 6), from the perspective of academics in accounting departments at universities in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and collected data through a 24-item questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, simple regression, and path analysis were conducted using SPSS. The sample comprised 165 academics. The results indicate a positive, statistically significant effect of the technologies under investigation on perceived professional competence (β = 0.745; R² = 0.555). The model accounts for 55.5% of the variance, while the remaining 44.5% is attributable to factors not included in the model. By technology, expert systems had the highest explanatory power (R² = 0.465), followed by machine learning (R² = 0.387) and blockchain (R² = 0.289). These findings reflect academics’ views and do not constitute a direct measurement of accountants’ actual competence. The study recommends updating accounting curricula to reflect technological developments and labor-market needs in alignment with IES 6.

Burnout has become a major occupational health concern in Japan, particularly under flexible work arrangements that may intensify self-regulatory demands. This study aimed to clarify the effects of self-endangering work behavior (SEWB) and other work-related psycho-behavioral factors on burnout among Japanese workers. An Internet-based cross-sectional survey was conducted with 800 participants (four groups of 200 each): two groups engaged in professional and planning work under a discretionary labor system, and two comparable groups of non-discretionary workers. The discretionary labor system in Japan allows employees greater autonomy over working hours while evaluating performance based on deemed working time rather than actual hours worked. Among professional workers, burnout (emotional impairment), SEWB, workaholism, and work engagement were significantly higher in discretionary compared with non-discretionary workers. Multiple regression analyses showed burnout was positively associated with SEWB and workaholism in both professional groups. Among planning workers, SEWB and work engagement were higher in discretionary workers, whereas burnout did not differ significantly. Burnout was positively associated with workaholism in both groups and with SEWB only in non-discretionary workers. These findings suggest differential risks of burnout depending on occupational type and labor system.

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed creative and analytical workflows. However, the ubiquitous, linear chat interfaces used to interact with these models operate as opaque "black boxes." This frictionless design paradigm obscures algorithmic processes, resulting in a severe loss of human agency, cognitive overload and a widespread disconnect from the environmental costs of computation. This thesis critiques the current state of AI interfaces and proposes a shift from passive automation to informed, transparent collaboration. Employing a Research-through-Design (RtD) methodology grounded in Explainable AI (XAI) and visual programming principles, this study investigates how interface design can bridge the cognitive gap between human intent and machine execution. The research introduces three distinct functional prototypes, each addressing a specific layer of transparency. First, it establishes "Systemic Transparency" by showing the real-world energy footprint of AI prompts to promote mindful consumption. Second, it explores "Cognitive Transparency" by acting as an interactive tutor rather than an automated editor, keeping users in control of their own learning. Finally, it achieves "Architectural Transparency" by ditching the standard text box for a spatial canvas, allowing users to map out their ideas and precisely control the AI's output. By synthesizing these interventions into a comprehensive Human-Centric AI Design Framework, this research demonstrates that transparency does not have to equal complexity. The findings conclude that the future of ethical and effective AI relies on replacing opaque automation with productive visibility, ensuring that as artificial intelligence scales, human creators remain the sovereign architects of their own work.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an increasingly influential technology in modern education. Its development has created new opportunities for improving the teaching and learning of English as a foreign language. AI-powered applications can support language learners by providing personalized exercises, immediate feedback, interactive communication, and access to additional learning resources. They can also assist teachers in preparing lesson materials, designing classroom activities, and identifying students' learning needs. However, the integration of AI into English language teaching presents several challenges, including the possibility of inaccurate information, excessive dependence on technology, privacy concerns, and unequal access to digital resources. This article examines the main applications of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and considers practical ways to integrate AI into language classrooms. It argues that artificial intelligence can improve the learning process when it is used responsibly and combined with effective teaching methods. The article emphasizes that teachers remain essential in developing students' communication skills, critical thinking, creativity, and intercultural awareness.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors (n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out (β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment (β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own (r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially (r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance (β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance (M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

documents.abstract: This study investigates how musicians who use generative artificial intelligence (genAI) conceptualize authority and authorship within their creative practices, situating these perspectives within broader historical contexts and legal frameworks. Reflecting a lineage of technologies that have historically disrupted the music ecosystem, this study examines genAI as the latest technology to challenge established paradigms regulating authority, authorship, and mediation. Much like prior innovations that problematized the relationships between creator, technology, and expressive work, genAI introduces new uncertainties regarding intentionality, control, and the locus of creative agency. Grounded in qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with musicians who actively incorporate genAI into their creative processes, this study seeks to understand how these practitioners interpret their own sense of autonomy in the production of genAI music and attachment to the music produced. In doing so, this study investigates whether authority and authorship can persist when onlookers characterize the circumstances of the creative process as unpredictable, opaque, and automated. The analysis is further informed by various theoretical lenses, including Aristotelian ethics and metaphysics, critical theory of technology, labor theory of property, and personality theory. By comparing musicians’ lived experiences with institutional definitions of authority and authorship, this study highlights potential gaps between musical practice and public policy, particularly in light of recent legal decisions that deny copyright protection to works lacking clear human authorship. As such, this study anticipates that musicians’ engagement with genAI may reveal complex understandings concerning authority and authorship that extend beyond the scope currently recognized within dominant legal frameworks.

Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

Polypharmacy requires drug–drug interaction risk to be assessed in relation to mechanism, severity, patient vulnerability, exposure, monitoring options, and clinical workflow. Feature-based methods, deep learning, knowledge graphs, multimodal fusion, and event-level models provide a computational foundation for predicting DDIs. Their clinical application also requires patient-specific interpretation and evaluation within the intended workflow. This narrative review examines how pairwise prediction can be integrated with these requirements in medication-safety systems. Multimodal biomedical foundation models may connect chemical structures, targets, pathways, knowledge graphs, literature, pharmacovigilance, real-world evidence, and patient trajectories. Large language models can assist with retrieval, summarization, explanation, and communication under source verification and professional review. Bounded AI agents may coordinate planning, tool use, verification, escalation, documentation, monitoring, and audit. We organize these components into a human-supervised architecture and an evaluation pathway linking model performance with workflow and clinical outcomes. Key challenges include data leakage, distribution shift, poorly documented evidence sources, hallucination, workflow burden, governance, and limited prospective validation. Prospective evaluations should assess how these systems affect medication decisions, monitoring, and patient outcomes, alongside the reliability of their evidence and the workload they create.

documents.abstract: This study characterizes baseline patterns of proxemic behavior in typically developing toddlers during a structured interaction with a social robot. Using overhead video and a convolutional neural network, we automatically identified the locations of the child, robot, and other individuals in the room and extracted distance-based measures throughout the interaction. These behavioral measures were analyzed alongside standardized developmental assessment scores to quantify variability within this normative sample. The combined data demonstrated substantial variability in children's proxemic behaviors, highlighting the range of ways young children engage with a novel robotic partner. These findings provide foundational descriptive data for early-childhood human-robot interaction and establish a methodological framework that future hypothesis-driven studies, including those involving clinically diagnosed populations, can build upon. No diagnostic or screening interpretations should be drawn from this work.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across public administrations, industry, education, and critical infrastructures is increasing demands for computational efficiency, transparency, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. While cloud-centric AI architectures have enabled major advances in machine learning, they face growing challenges related to data movement, latency, energy consumption, explainability, cybersecurity, and digital sovereignty. At the same time, European regulatory frameworks such as the European AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, the Data Act, and the Data Governance Act impose heterogeneous requirements concerning AI risk management, data protection, cybersecurity, data governance, accountability, and access to data. Current research addresses Edge Computing, Neuro-Symbolic AI, Knowledge Graphs, Explainable AI, and Sustainable AI largely as separate domains. This paper introduces SOFIA (Sovereign, Ontology-driven Framework for Intelligent Action), a conceptual knowledge-driven neuro-symbolic framework that integrates Edge-Cloud Continuum principles, Data Gravity, Knowledge Graphs, and Governance-by-Design mechanisms. SOFIA aims to define and operationalize the concept of Knowledge Gravity, extending compute-to-data approaches by considering the placement of semantic knowledge, reasoning capabilities, policies, and regulatory constraints closer to the points where decisions are generated across the continuum. Through the integration of machine learning, symbolic reasoning, and evolving Knowledge Graphs, the framework outlines how explainable and governance-aware intelligence could be deployed on resource-constrained edge devices while reducing reliance on centralized infrastructures. In this perspective, Knowledge Gravity is proposed as a conceptual orchestration principle for distributed cognition, where knowledge assets influence placement and governance decisions. To illustrate the proposed concepts, the paper introduces a preliminary mathematical formulation and a synthetic simulation based on hypothetical deployment scenarios. These examples are intended only to demonstrate the behavior of the proposed indicators and optimization perspective and do not constitute empirical validation of the framework. By framing knowledge placement, reasoning availability, governance requirements, and sovereignty constraints within a unified architectural perspective, SOFIA contributes a research agenda for distributed, explainable, and sustainable AI across the Edge-Cloud Continuum. The framework is presented as a conceptual foundation whose assumptions, metrics, and expected benefits require future validation in real-world deployments.

Digital transformation has redefined Human Talent Management by incorporating analytical tools capable of converting large volumes of data into strategic information for decision-making. In this context, People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence represent key innovations for optimizing recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, talent retention, and workforce planning.This study aimed to analyze how the integration of these technologies transforms decision-making in Human Talent Management within Panamanian organizations and to propose a strategic analytical maturity model adapted to the national context. A qualitative research approach with descriptive, explanatory, and propositional scope was employed, supported by a systematic review of scientific literature, documentary analysis, and the conceptual design of the Panamanian People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Maturity Model (MPM-PAIA). The findings indicate that organizations with greater analytical capabilities improve strategic decision-making, strengthen the efficiency of human resource processes, and enhance competitiveness. Data quality, leadership, organizational culture, analytical competencies, and ethical governance were identified as critical success factors. The study concludes that the progressive integration of People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence represents a strategic opportunity for Panamanian organizations, provided that technological adoption is accompanied by workforce development and ethical governance.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies has significantly transformed language teaching and learning in the twenty-first century. Traditional approaches to language education are increasingly complemented by intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment tools, and generative AI applications. These innovations create new opportunities for personalized instruction, interactive learning, and the development of learners’ communicative competence. This article examines the transformational stages of integrating artificial intelligence and digital technologies into language teaching. It explores the transition from traditional classroom instruction to technology-enhanced learning, intelligent and adaptive education, and AI-supported personalized learning environments. Particular attention is paid to the pedagogical benefits, practical challenges, and ethical considerations associated with the implementation of these technologies. The article argues that successful digital transformation requires not only technological innovation but also pedagogically grounded implementation, teacher training, digital literacy, and responsible use of AI.

The rapid spread of artificial intelligence-based technologies has made trust a fundamental element in the sustainable adoption of these technologies. This study aimed to adapt the Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Technologies Trust Scale developed by Nazaretsky et al. (2022b) into Turkish in the context of prospective teachers and to examine its psychometric validity and reliability. Data were collected from 423 undergraduate students enrolled in various programs at a state university. The factor structure of the scale was analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The fit indices of the initial 25-item model fell below acceptable thresholds. Repeated analyses resulted in a three-factor, 21-item solution. This final structure is consistent with the original dimensions, named Perceived Benefits, Perceived Barriers/Concerns, and Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies. The fit indices for the final model were found to be acceptable (e.g., χ2/df = 1.425, RMSEA = 0.052, SRMR = 0.061). The Cronbach's alpha internal consistency coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.803. The Cronbach's alpha coefficients for the subscales were 0.813, 0.684, and 0.811, respectively. Convergent and discriminant validity analyses showed that the scale is valid and reliable in its current form. These findings lay the groundwork for creating a standardized framework for monitoring and comparing trust in AI-based educational technologies among educators, policymakers, and researchers in Türkiye.

We present a two-stage AI-enabled framework for enhancing operator situational awareness during compressed hydrogen bunkering in maritime confined spaces. In the event of a leak, the framework first estimates the unknown leakage rate from early sensor readings and then forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will disperse over the next time steps, providing operators with a predicted concentration map together with confidence bounds. The framework is based on two independent AI models building one AI system. The AI system is designed as a decision-support tool. It augments sensor readings, and thus enhances operator situational awareness and supports decision-making. This enables preventive safety barriers to be deployed before hazardous concentrations are reached, while an independent emergency shutdown system remains the ultimate safety layer. The system design incorporates safeguards to ensure the AI system operates within its competence envelope. On an open dataset of confined-space hydrogen releases, the independent AI models achieve a mean absolute error of 0.052 g/s in leakage-rate estimation and ≈ 0 . 0 1 8 in hydrogen-concentration prediction, approaching the sensor precision bound of ± 0 . 0 1 . The combined end-to-end framework achieves a mean absolute error of ≈ 0 . 0 2 5 in hydrogen-concentration prediction. The hydrogen-concentration prediction provides calibrated uncertainty estimates that allow operators to judge the reliability of each forecast. These results suggest that the framework may provide early information about hazardous concentration build-up, potentially supporting preventive actions by operators.

This qualitative case study explores how primary school educators in Cyprus integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into their teaching and professional practice within an education system at an early stage of AI adoption. Data were collected from fifteen educators through semi-structured interviews, concurrent think-aloud protocols, and AI-supported lesson plans. The data were analysed using an expanded Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), incorporating selected constructs from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the AI-TPACK framework to examine individual, organisational, and contextual influences on AI adoption. Findings indicate that educators integrated AI into lesson planning, instructional differentiation, assessment design, multimedia development, and self-directed professional learning. Although participants demonstrated increasing confidence and professional agency in using AI, sustained implementation depended less on individual willingness than on the availability of organisational, pedagogical, and policy support. Limited infrastructure, fragmented professional development, ethical uncertainty, inconsistent leadership, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance constrained the transition from individual experimentation to systematic classroom integration. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI in primary education by demonstrating that meaningful AI implementation in early-adoption education systems is shaped by the interaction between teacher agency and institutional conditions rather than by technology acceptance alone. Based on these findings, a five-pillar framework is proposed to support responsible and sustainable AI integration through systemic governance, equitable access, embedded professional learning, curriculum and pedagogical alignment, and stakeholder engagement. While grounded in the Cypriot context, the findings offer insights that may inform AI implementation in comparable education systems.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study examines key factors influencing the learning performance of Physical Education majors at a public vocational college in Henan Province and evaluates the effectiveness of a blended learning intervention. Research design, data and methodology: An Intervention Design and Implementation (IDI) framework with pre-IDI, IDI, and post-IDI stages was applied using mixed methods. Content validity and reliability were confirmed through expert review and a pilot test. Survey data from 80 students were analyzed using multiple linear regression. A 12-week blended learning intervention was then implemented with 40 students, followed by paired-sample t-tests and supportive interviews. Results: Regression analysis showed that behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement, learning motivation, active collaborative learning, and feedback significantly predicted learning performance, with feedback showing the strongest effect (β = 0.324). Paired-sample t-test results indicated significant improvements across all variables after the intervention, including learning performance (mean difference = 0.45). Interview findings aligned with the quantitative results, indicating higher engagement, motivation, collaboration, and more effective feedback use. Conclusions: The findings demonstrate that blended learning supported by structured pedagogy can significantly enhance learning performance in Physical Education. By embedding key learning principles into instructional design, this approach strengthens both learning processes and outcomes. The study provides empirical and theoretical insights for improving blended learning in vocational education contexts.

Learn how to identify who or what is interacting with your application using AgentCredia's Actor Classes Reference Card. This practical resource explains the four actor classifications: Human, Human + AI, Agent, and Unknown, along with the evidence used to support each classification. Understand the difference between verified, declared, inferred, and unknown evidence, why account authentication does not establish actor identity, and how to interpret AI agent activity without making unsupported assumptions. Ideal for SaaS platforms, API developers, security teams, and organizations preparing for AI-driven interactions.

Trong bối cảnh Việt Nam đang thúc đẩy phát triển ngành công nghiệp bán dẫn nhằm tham gia sâu hơn vào chuỗi giá trị công nghệ toàn cầu, việc thu hút và phát triển nguồn nhân lực kỹ thuật chất lượng cao trở thành yêu cầu cấp thiết. Tuy nhiên, các nghiên cứu hiện nay chủ yếu tập trung vào nhu cầu nhân lực và khoảng cách kỹ năng, trong khi cơ chế hình thành ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp trong lĩnh vực bán dẫn của sinh viên kỹ thuật vẫn chưa được làm rõ. Dựa trên Lý thuyết Nhận thức Nghề nghiệp Xã hội (SCCT), nghiên cứu này phân tích tác động của niềm tin vào năng lực bản thân (SEF) đến ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp trong ngành bán dẫn, đồng thời làm rõ vai trò của nhận thức về đặc điểm công việc (JOB) và sự phù hợp giữa cá nhân và công việc (PJF). Dữ liệu được thu thập từ 448 sinh viên năm cuối thuộc các ngành kỹ thuật tại Việt Nam và được phân tích bằng phương pháp PLS-SEM. Kết quả cho thấy SEF có ảnh hưởng tích cực đến JOB (β = 0,574), PJF (β = 0,362) và ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp (β = 0,464). Đồng thời, JOB tác động tích cực đến PJF (β = 0,362), trong khi PJF ảnh hưởng đáng kể đến ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp (β = 0,244). Nghiên cứu cho thấy nhận thức về đặc điểm công việc và sự phù hợp giữa cá nhân và công việc là các cơ chế nhận thức quan trọng giúp chuyển hóa niềm tin vào năng lực bản thân thành ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp trong lĩnh vực bán dẫn. Nghiên cứu đã mở rộng ứng dụng SCCT trong bối cảnh ngành công nghệ cao thông qua việc làm rõ vai trò của JOB và PJF đối với ý định lựa chọn nghề nghiệp của sinh viên kỹ thuật tại Việt Nam.

Lightweight virtual reality (VR) can visually specify self-motion without body translation, but compact systems cannot readily reproduce body-scale forces. We tested whether ungrounded asymmetric vibration intended to evoke pulling changes maximum self-motion-speed ratings. Twenty-four adults completed a primary and a secondary within-participant experiment. In Experiment 1, optic flow at 10 or 15 m/s was presented alone, with symmetric vibration, or with asymmetric vibration whose perceived pull was velocity-aligned or velocity-opposed to visually specified self-motion. Both asymmetric mappings produced higher ratings than the visual-only and symmetric-vibration controls, whereas the mappings did not reliably differ. In Experiment 2, adding self-motion-specifying optic flow in the velocity-aligned configuration increased maximum-pulling-force ratings relative to haptic-only stimulation. A direct configuration-by-rating-type interaction showed that this effect was larger for pulling-force than vibration-intensity ratings obtained from the same trials. The tested pseudo-traction configurations thus changed reported self-motion magnitude, while Experiment 2 provided complementary rating-specificity evidence. Because asymmetric and symmetric stimulation also differed in waveform-dependent properties, the results are consistent with, but do not isolate, a contribution of the perceived pulling sensation. They do not establish a universal directional-mapping rule or a direct change in vection dynamics. For lightweight VR design, cue magnitude and force meaning are separable design decisions.

Despite growing generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption in language teaching, how teachers of languages other than English (LOTEs) navigate GAI integration remains understudied. The study combines grounded-theory analysis with fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) of 18 university LOTE teacher cases recruited through purposive and theoretical sampling. Grounded theory generated a model of factors influencing LOTE teachers’ engagement with GAI, and fsQCA identified four high-engagement configurations organized into two solution families. A supplementary qualitative account highlighted reservations concerning GAI’s pedagogical compatibility. The findings illustrate that GAI reproduces, rather than eliminates, the existing linguistic hierarchies in LOTE language education and theorize adaptive labor of LOTE teachers not just as a signal of high engagement but of deliberate, expertise-driven response to asymmetrical GAI tool design that privileges high-resource languages. This reframes GAI adoption as a linguistic equity issue with implications for differentiated professional development and equitable tool design.

Smartphones are frequently used in stationary (i.e., static) contexts where users place them on surfaces for extended periods to support tasks such as following recipe instructions while cooking, accessing manuals while repairing, or practicing crafts like painting or pottery through video. However, interacting with a smartphone in these scenarios often requires direct touchscreen contact, which becomes problematic to execute easily when both of the user’s hands get wet, greasy, or contaminated with substances such as oils and chemicals. This is because it can cause liquid ingress or display staining when touching the smartphone, as well as the triggering of technical faults such as “ghost touches” or screen non-responsiveness due to the presence of wet or contaminated insulating material. Existing solutions face limitations: voice control struggles with environmental noise, while Back-of-Device interactions are inaccessible when the smartphone is placed on a surface. Accordingly, we introduce Unobtrusive Ferromagnetic Objects (UFO)—a lightweight, passive solution that enables touch-free interaction with smartphones using readily available ferromagnetic (FM) objects found in everyday settings in various forms, e.g., keys, spoons, screwdrivers, pens, and scales. UFO requires no modifications to the smartphone, object, environment, or surface, as it operates entirely through the built-in magnetometer. We conducted comprehensive technical and user-based (N=12) evaluations of the UFO technique across a wide range of real-world scenarios. The results demonstrated highly accurate identification of FM object-based inputs (98.9% on average) without requiring prior calibration, while maintaining consistent performance across diverse real world environments. Additionally, a user study (N = 21) demonstrated that the UFO approach achieved high task performance and low reported difficulty and fatigue when compared with direct touchscreen interaction under the matched temporal-gesture condition. These findings support the feasibility of UFO for providing touch-free input to smartphones placed on surfaces and motivate potential applications in situations where direct contact with the smartphone may be undesirable, including scenarios involving gloved or contaminated hands. By leveraging everyday objects as input tools, UFO presents an intuitive, scalable, and user-friendly alternative that complements traditional touchscreen interaction.

Feedback is an important interaction channel in human–robot collaboration (HRC), yet feedback solicitation may affect users independently of whether their feedback changes robot behavior. This between-subjects study investigated how user-initiated and system-prompted feedback influence short-term trust development and perceived safety in a virtual industrial collaboration task. Forty-eight participants were assigned to either a system-prompted condition (n = 23), in which feedback was requested at predefined task milestones, or a user-initiated condition (n = 25), in which feedback could be provided at self-selected moments. Trust was assessed before and after the interaction, while perceived safety was measured afterward. A mixed ANCOVA revealed a significant time-by-condition interaction: trust increased in the system-prompted condition, compared to the user-initiated condition. Perceived safety did not differ between conditions. These findings suggest that feedback solicitation may function as an interaction-design feature that may shape short-term trust and feedback coverage under stable robot behavior.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly influential component of contemporary education, creating new opportunities for improving English language teaching methodology. AI-powered applications can support lesson planning, instructional material development, personalized learning, pronunciation practice, writing assessment, vocabulary acquisition, and the development of communicative competence. At the same time, their integration into educational practice raises important questions concerning pedagogical effectiveness, academic integrity, data privacy, teacher autonomy, and learners’ critical thinking. This article examines the methodological applications of artificial intelligence tools in English language teaching, focusing on their educational potential, practical implementation, and associated challenges. The study employs a qualitative, literature-based methodology drawing on research in educational technology, computer-assisted language learning, artificial intelligence, and English language pedagogy. The analysis identifies major areas in which AI can support teachers and learners, including lesson design, differentiated instruction, interactive communication, automated feedback, and formative assessment. It also examines the importance of teacher mediation, digital literacy, and responsible technology use.

Metro operators worldwide face critical fail-to-board events at centralised interchange stations, where local mitigation (e.g., schedule adjustments or empty-train insertion) can displace congestion downstream. We propose a calibrated digital twin of the Panama Metro integrated with two AI optimisation methods: a genetic algorithm and a deep reinforcement learning agent. Using real operational data from morning peak hours, the framework evaluates dispatching policies to minimise network-wide fail-to-board and is benchmarked against manual control and a commercial solver with station-level targets. The commercial solver reduced fail-to-board at Central Station by 37% but required 8–18 min per optimisation. The genetic algorithm achieved comparable reduction (33%) in 60–120 s while optimising network-wide performance. Deep reinforcement learning reached similar performance (32%) with $$\sim $$ ∼ 1 s inference, enabling near-real-time deployment in metro control rooms. Unlike station-level optimisation, network-wide optimisation prevents congestion displacement to upstream stations, resulting in lower spillover while maintaining similar fail-to-board reduction across the entire network.

Written intercultural communication is an essential competence for university students who study and work in linguistically and culturally diverse environments. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can support this competence by providing timely language feedback, modelling alternative registers, helping learners consider audience expectations, and enabling iterative revision. However, fluent AI-generated text does not automatically develop intercultural understanding: systems may reproduce cultural stereotypes, overlook local context, or encourage overreliance. This article examines pedagogical ways of integrating AI into the teaching of written intercultural communication in higher education. Following an integrative, concept-oriented review of relevant scholarship, it proposes a classroom framework that combines AI-supported input, guided drafting, intercultural peer review, and human reflection. A practical matrix links learning objectives, AI-supported activities, and assessment criteria. The article argues that AI should function as a scaffold rather than an author, with transparent use, privacy protection, source checking, and student ownership built into course design. The proposed framework offers a practical basis for lesson planning and future empirical evaluation.

The expressive exploration of sonic spaces is a frequent mechanism of Digital Musical Instruments. These spaces can consist in sets of sounds, sonified data, interpolated synthesis presets and so on. Performers, whether novices or experts, might find it difficult to navigate such spaces due to their complexity and diversity. Extended Reality technologies enable the addition of visual elements over the physical space, providing visual feedback on the sonic space using colours, shapes or visual metaphors. However, it can be challenging to display the information without visual overload and while preserving the focus on musical gestures. In this article, we investigate different types of visualisations for the exploration of sonic spaces in Mixed Reality. We use drawing as an interaction metaphor, with strokes as a visual representation of a sonic trajectory. After evaluating various feedback options in a study with expert musical and visual artists, we conduct a controlled experiment with 18 novice users. The task was to reproduce sequences of sounds inside a sonic space by doing trajectories, while testing out different visualisation levels directly onto the strokes. The results did not reveal a statistically significant effect of the visualisations on the trajectories’ accuracy (with only anecdotal evidence for an absence of difference). However, participants preferred having higher levels of visualisation to guide them in their sonic exploration.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed educational practices worldwide, with artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as one of the most influential tools in reshaping teaching and learning; yet instructional delivery in many higher education science classrooms remains predominantly lecture-based. An investigative study on the awareness and utilization of artificial intelligence in the instructional delivery of Biology education at Akwa Ibom State University, Nigeria, was conducted using a descriptive survey research design. Three research questions and a hypothesis guided the study. The population of the study consisted of 923 students from level 200-400 in the entire program in the Department of Education, Akwa Ibom State University. A Sample of 234 students was selected using Taro Yamane’s formula. Awareness of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (AAIQ) and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (UAIQ) was developed, with a reliability coefficient will be determined using Cronbach's alpha. Hard copy of the questionnaires will be administered to respondents. Frequency counts, mean, standard deviation, and one-way ANOVA were used to analyze the data obtained. Results showed that a significant difference existed in the level of awareness of Artificial Intelligence among Biology Education students across the different academic levels; result also indicate that a statistically significant difference existed in the level of utilization of Artificial Intelligence among Biology Education students across the different academic levels, and male students used Artificial Intelligence more compared to their female counterparts. Based on the findings, it was recommended, among others, that tertiary institutions and governments should integrate the utilization of Artificial Intelligence among students in other to have appropriate knowledge and skills to meet with increasing globalization and needs of society.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Despite continued advances in smart glasses’ display capabilities, on-device touch input remains fundamentally constrained by the thin temple form factor and its narrow, primarily horizontal input space. In this work, we present VertiTouch, a novel system that vertically expands the touch input space of thin temples of smart glasses, directly enabling self-contained dexterous 2D touch interaction. Rather than restricting contact to the fingertip, VertiTouch leverages the entire finger to extend the 6 mm vertical input axis to the length of the finger. We implemented a system prototype through iterative refinements and evaluated it in two controlled studies with 12 participants using a Fitts’ law-style 2D target selection task spanning 36.2° × 36.2° visual angle. With high-precision external tracking, VertiTouch performed within approximately 10% of a physically large 70 × 50 mm temple touchpad representing an upper-bound reference for on-device touch area, both in mean target selection time and throughput estimate. Using only compact on-device sensors, the standalone prototype achieved a mean selection time of 2.4 s on the same task. Overall, our findings demonstrate that self-contained rich 2D touch input is possible on smart glasses alone by virtually extending the vertical input space along the index finger.

Digital learning technologies offer expanding opportunities for higher education, yet little is known about how immersive virtual reality (VR), traditional 2D video, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-generated podcasts compare in content-equivalent settings. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and Self-Efficacy Theory, this study examined effects of medium on short-term knowledge acquisition, motivation, perceived agency, and self-efficacy. German university students were randomly assigned to VR, 2D video, or an AI-generated podcast and engaged with equivalent content on the history of the German National Theatre in Weimar for approximately 6 min. A pre-post design assessed changes across outcomes. The medium produced no significant differences in knowledge acquisition or self-efficacy, and most directional expectations were unsupported. A small effect emerged for a composite affective measure (partial η2 = 0.072), favoring VR over 2D video, while VR and the AI-generated podcast did not differ significantly. As no formal equivalence test was conducted, non-significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. The findings provide preliminary evidence that AI-generated podcasts may represent a low-cost, scalable option for higher education, although conclusions are limited to one short intervention, one topic, one AI platform, and immediate post-exposure outcomes. Further research should examine broader contexts.

In 3D environments, factors such as hand and tracker jitter can substantially degrade user performance during ray-casting selection. This makes it difficult for users to complete selection tasks involving target objects with small visible areas, since small targets require higher levels of precision. This paper proposes VoroCast —a Voronoi-based two-stage selection technique designed for dense environments in VR, aimed at reducing the precision required for the task. In the first stage, VoroCast captures candidate objects via cone casting; then it dynamically generates a semi-transparent disambiguation disc based on Voronoi partitioning. VoroCast, based on Voronoi partitioning, mathematically guarantees a nearest-neighbor-based selection area for each candidate object’s selection area, which enlarges the effective target width relevant to Fitts’ Law and thereby reduces pointing difficulty. To evaluate the performance of VoroCast, we recruited participants to compare it against two state-of-the-art techniques in dense virtual scenes. The results demonstrate that VoroCast achieves significant advantages in selection efficiency, accuracy, and user preference.

Virtual sensing can reduce the cost of generating sensor datasets for human activity recognition and ubiquitous sensing, yet users must still translate sensing intent into concrete scene configurations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to translate sensing goals into concrete configurations and refine them as results emerge. We present VsensAgent, a human–agent interface that grounds an LLM-powered agent in a shared 3D simulation environment. Users combine natural-language delegation with direct scene manipulation, while the agent can inspect scene state, configure sensors and avatar motions, record data, and support signal analysis. We conducted a task-based study of VsensAgent in which 12 participants completed 36 virtual sensing authoring sessions. Analysis of interaction logs, authored configurations, and post-task interviews showed that participants progressively developed intent through executable scene states, shifted control between agent delegation and direct manipulation at the level of individual operations, and treated agent proposals as editable starting points. These findings frame virtual sensor generation as progressive, collaborative authoring and inform the design of agents for stateful workflows.

The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education raises concerns about students’ cognitive atrophy, as many students are tempted to delegate tasks that require deep reasoning to GenAI. This study examines university students’ perceptions of Minimalist, a dialogic AI assistant designed to scaffold a discourse synthesis task through a specific discourse architecture, and asks them to engage in critical thinking while doing the task, rather than generating content for them. Twenty-three university students interacted with Minimalist during a single-session discourse synthesis task, after which they completed an open-ended questionnaire. Inductive thematic analysis revealed six themes. Findings demonstrate that dialogic scaffolding was experienced as pedagogically valuable and yielded three design principles, the Dialogic Scaffolding Principle, the Dialogic Threshold, and the Automation-Cognition Balance Problem, with implications for the future design of educational AI systems.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can suggest wording, explain language, and increasingly contribute to feedback and assessment. The central issue is not only what these systems generate, but when learners, teachers, and institutions begin to treat their outputs as reasons for judging language. Existing research addresses language ideology, distributed agency, algorithmic normativity, trust, assessment, and AI governance, but these literatures use different concepts for influence, authority, and institutional power. This article develops a multilevel framework of linguistic authority escalation through a critical integrative review focused primarily on English-dominant higher-education writing and assessment. In the framework, authority in the strict sense refers to attributed epistemic or normative standing; operational uptake is causal influence, and regulatory consequentiality is institutional power. The framework differentiates the initiator, subject, decision-maker, and accountable actor, and represents the source of authorisation, the subject’s degree of meaningful choice, and the durability of system embedding as co-occurring configurational conditions rather than alternative routes. It also distinguishes epistemic warrant, procedural legitimacy, substantive linguistic justice, and assessment validity as different standards for evaluating AI-mediated judgement. A literature-grounded worked case shows how the same model suggestion can remain optional assistance or acquire institutional force depending on these relations. The framework helps educational linguists identify when GenAI support preserves evaluative control and when opaque linguistic norms become difficult to contest, directing pedagogy and governance towards norm-explicit feedback, meaningful alternatives, task-specific evidence, appeal, and clear answerability.

Artificial intelligence safety research compares systems' answers and actions with output probabilities, generated reasoning, internal activations and monitoring judgments. These measurements can disagree about what a system knows, what influenced its response and whether unwanted behavior occurred. This critical tutorial review organizes the emerging literature around five comparisons: relative sensitivity, incremental value, functional dissociation, causal intervention and targeted robustness. Worked examples distinguish reported findings, their inferential limits and informative follow-up comparisons. The comparisons are introduced through simpler settings and then applied where models respond to evaluation, withhold capabilities or make other evidence less revealing. Three conclusions connect research on knowledge elicitation, reasoning faithfulness, evaluation awareness, deliberate underperformance and monitoring. Measurements that agree under one condition need not remain interchangeable under another. Failure to recover information does not by itself establish its removal. And a measurement's usefulness belongs to the complete procedure and the conditions of use, including opportunities to influence the evidence. Human research on perception, memory, verbal reports and concealed information supplies methodological resources without any assumption of shared mechanisms. Three concrete extensions of existing experiments illustrate controlled relearning after unlearning, the information a reasoning report adds beyond an observer, and adaptation against individual monitors and their combination. An experiment-level source guide supports the synthesis. The aim is to make dissociations useful for cumulative safety research: not merely as differences between scores, but as evidence that changes an interpretation or determines the next informative experiment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.
